name: Kingdom of Scotland
summary: The kingdom in northern Britain traditionally founded by Kenneth MacAlpin (843); it kept its independence from England in the wars of the 1300s, shared a king with England from 1603 and united with it in 1707.

location.value: Orkney and Shetland were incorporated in 1472, annexed from Norway.

terrain.value: Mountainous Highlands and islands in the north and west, fertile Central Lowlands, and the hilly Southern Uplands.

climate.value: Cool, wet and windy; colder years in the 1600s, during the Little Ice Age, brought harvest failures.

resources.value: Wool, hides and cattle, herring and salmon, coal and salt, and oats and barley grown in the Lowlands.

population.value: About 500,000 (1500), 800,000 (1600) and 1,250,000 (1700) per the infobox; hearth-tax returns for 1691 indicate 1,234,575.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; royal burghs grew as trading towns, led by Edinburgh, with Glasgow, Aberdeen, Dundee and Perth.

disease.value: The Black Death reached Scotland in 1349, and plague returned many times until the 1640s.

migration.value: Thousands of Scots settled in Ulster from 1609; others went as soldiers and traders to Poland and Sweden.

economicBase.value: The fertile Central Lowlands supported most farming and towns, while the Highlands and Southern Uplands were less productive. The currency was the Pound Scots (the Bank of Scotland issued notes from 1704), and the 1690s brought severe economic dislocation. Oats, cattle, sheep, fishing and wool exports are not detailed in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with the Low Countries and Scandinavia.

wealth.value: Much poorer than England; the failure of the Darien scheme around 1700 cost a large share of the country’s capital.

moneyAndTax.value: The pound Scots, which lost value over time and was worth one-twelfth of a pound sterling by 1707.

inequality.value: Great nobles, lairds and clan chiefs held the land; tenants, cottars and labourers paid rents in kind and service.

governmentType.value: The page says Parliament was never as central to national life as England’s; it does not describe three estates.

keyRulers.value: Cínaed mac Ailpín (Kenneth MacAlpin) became king of the Picts in the 840s, traditionally 843; Robert I’s parliament at Scone enacted a code of law in 1318; James VI inherited the English and Irish thrones in 1603.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Scotland (checked 13 Nov 2026); scotland.org: History (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Robert the Bruce crowned 1306; James VI inherited the English throne in 1603)

succession.value: Hereditary in the royal line: the House of Bruce from 1306, and the Stewart dynasty from 1371 to 1707.

institutions.value: The Parliament of Scotland, the Privy Council, the Court of Session (1532) and, from 1560, the Church of Scotland (Kirk).

stability.value: Often unsettled: many kings came to the throne as children, and James I (1437) and James III (1488) were killed.

eliteConflict.value: Feuds among great noble families such as the Douglases, and among Highland clans such as the Campbells and MacDonalds.

armyAndTech.value: Spearmen in schiltron formations won at Bannockburn (1314); later armies used cannon such as Mons Meg and Highland charges.

majorWars.value: Battle of Bannockburn (1314), an English defeat.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Scotland (checked 13 Nov 2026); scotland.org: History (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Bruce defeated Edward II at Bannockburn in 1314)

territoryChange.value: Gained the Western Isles from Norway (1266) and Orkney and Shetland (1472), but lost Berwick to England in 1482.

alliancesRivals.value: The Auld Alliance with France from 1295, against the long rivalry with England.

inventions.value: John Napier published his invention of logarithms in 1614, which made complex calculations much faster.

scienceEducation.value: Universities: St Andrews (1413), Glasgow, Aberdeen, Edinburgh.

openness.value: Open to Europe through trade with the Low Countries, France and the Baltic, and students studying abroad.

communicationTransport.value: Ships along the coasts and to Europe; cattle walked south on drove roads, and inland roads were poor.

religion.value: By 1560 a small group of Protestants was able to impose reform on the Scottish church.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Scotland (checked 13 Nov 2026); scotland.org: History (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Mary’s reign (from 1542) saw conflict between Catholics and Protestants; the page does not name the 1560 Reformation)

languageWriting.value: Gaelic in the Highlands, Scots in the Lowlands, Norn in Orkney and Shetland, and Latin and English in writing.

artsArchitecture.value: Castles such as Edinburgh and Stirling, abbeys such as Melrose, and poets (makars) such as Robert Henryson and William Dunbar.

socialStructure.value: Clans in the Highlands; burghs in the Lowlands.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared sense of independence from England, expressed in the Declaration of Arbroath (1320).

dailyLife.value: Most people farmed in small townships, ate oatmeal and kale, kept cattle and burned peat for warmth.

neighbours.value: England to the south, Ireland across the North Channel, Norway (which held the northern isles until 1468–69) and France as ally.

ideasReligions.value: Presbyterian Protestantism after John Knox and the 1560 Reformation; the National Covenant of 1638 defended it.

riseSignals.value: Traditionally dated to 843, when Kenneth MacAlpin became king of the Picts.

peakPeriod.value: James IV was killed when the Scots were beaten at Flodden in 1513; the page does not give 1488 or the 1508 printing press.

declineSignals.value: The Darien disaster (1698–1700) bankrupted many investors and helped push Scotland into union with England.

outcome.value: Union of the Crowns in 1603 (a personal union with England) and the Acts of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Scotland (checked 13 Nov 2026); scotland.org: History (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Union of the Crowns 1603; Act of Union 1707 created a single parliament for Great Britain at Westminster)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
